commentBody:
"Hope you enjoyed — I’ll be back soon!"

I did, Rafa! Thank you. 
Nice one. Fun Friday clues. 
Looking forward to more.
Nice Friday. Definitely more in line with what I assume are most folks’ expectations for the day of the week.

Still doing this puzzle, but came here to complain that when I click on a square, its border is boldened -- and this was appropriate for the Scrabble themed puzzle yesterday but was clearly not turned off for today's puzzle by whatever genius the Games people hire to do those things. Techies, I hear Doge is looking for people like you!

OK, back to the puzzle. Maybe I can turn off overlays or toggle something that'll take care of the problem. Or have they been emboldened all along and I just became aware of this? Is this all a dream?
Happy 1000 day streak to my mom & me - we decided to do the NYT crossword every day in Jan 2024… and never stopped! Love you mom!
Slow one today.

IKIDYOUNOT, this was a wonderful Friday puzzle, chock full of twisty clues and fun entries.  I always felt challenged, but never panicked throughout the solve. Favorite clues were those for GARAGEBANDS, MEDITATION, and ENEMYSPIES.

Does anybody still call marijuana MARYJANE?  The last time I heard that term was back in the 70s when my mother, of all people, told me that James Taylor’s reference to Mary Jane (in Suite for 20 G) was a reference to pot.
I'm sure I've solved a previous crossword from Rafael Musa. Something about the clues really irritates me. Is it just me?
This was far too easy for a Friday. Or maybe I'm just getting smarter. I would have liked a little more resistance.
Reading Elena Ferrante’s third Neapolitan book as we speak.  Nino turning into his dad.
Nice one
Pretty good puzzle with some lively answers and appropriately hard cluing, but perhaps too much traction/gimmes for a Friday.

Worth the wait, Rafael. Wonder what held it up so long?

About a perfect Friday to me. A good challenge where I had to use all the grid and finally get back the NW, where DINNERDATES stumped me for a bit. Nothing held me up for too long but there were few gimmes. Fun clues all around and no sour notes. Definitely Weintraubian.

I like the loophole connection. Gotta learn that skosh means a BIT and not to scotch something (cancel it). And ants live in a NEST not just a farm or hill. And that not just ASIA is distorted on a Mercator projection.

Thanks for helping me remember my grandmother’s kitchen. Knife, fork, plate, spoon, dish—no no no. Glass-doesn’t fit and anyway those could be used for either (depends on your practice). Oven? No of course not. SINK—finally! Although to be honest I think she had to make do with one in her small apartment. Never owned their own place, everything went to make sure the children and grandchildren had whatever they needed. May her memory be a blessing.

THAT REMINDS ME, and I KIDYOUNOT— Cincinnatians all know this but here in the Queen City “Please?” means “I didn’t hear you, can you repeat that?” I remember moving here and wondering why all these people were so polite all the time. They were just hard of hearing.

Anyway lots of fond memories and lovely connections in this puzzle. Thanks!
IMO pitched just right for a Friday.  No gimmes - well OK a long dead neuron twitched for Mary Jane; and Saigon of course but little apart from that.

Nice speedy puzzle and amazingly not outdated  by the publishing delay!     
lol GARAGEBAND and TINDERDATE.    And everyone playing Spelling Bee knows CELLI, so no worries there.
Enjoyed the puzzle but still don't get 50A. I got it with crossing entries but don't understand how the answer fits the clue.

Oral health crossing Tinder date? Swipes right for that one worthy crossing! 

Also enjoyed stewing on the spoon (cuddle) / ladle combo. 

And this reminds me, I kid you not, that a nice cold bottle of Gremona (vino cava) will put a little PEP in your vena cava. 

And I don't know why I find this worth sharing, but if I were to meet Ms. Shawkat on a Tinder date in Nantes, it would be reported in the society pages as John Ezra et Alia. 

When I was a kid (I kid you not) I mispronounced banal to rhyme with αnαl until in third grade Ms. Dines kindly told me to think of a canal when I wanted to say banal. But now when I say or write banal, I think of Ms. Dines. Freud would say I'm stuck at the oral stage and need some oral health.  What's an eight year old going around pronouncing some things banal? Hey, I'm among cruciverbalists here, and I'm sure a goodly number of you were slingin' around polysyllabics while still in the cradle!
This was a nicely seasoned easened.

At one time, I was convinced that the only way to do a crossword was to know every minor river on every continent.  

Now, it seems the way to do a crossword is to know absolutely everything there is to know about Taylor Swift...lyrics, nicknames, tour names...

I thought this was a pretty demanding puzzle.  Almost nothing came cheaply, and I bounced around the various sections of the puzzle several times before I got any of them completed.

In fact, I'm still not sure what [Stew on it!] has to do with LADLE, other than the easiest way to get stew from one place to another is with a ladle.

Nor can I fathom how the hull one maneuvers a CANOE on a ski slope.  I had to backpaddle on 1A several times before I finally fathomed it.

I found this an enjoyable puzzle with more misdirection than one can expect of NYT puzzles these days. I thought "Invasive plants" was a very cool clue, even if it unpleasantly reminded me of Russian acts of sabotage on Polish and European soil. My solve time between Wednesday and Thursday indicates experienced solvers probably found this a Tuesday though 🤣

I found the SE section especially challenging and I was close to throwing in the towel there. I managed to resolve everything on my own in the end, of which I am somewhat proud.

PCP was completely alien to me - I only know it as the name of a psychoactive drug. What is it short for? I suppose it's the American equivalent of the Polish "lekarz POZ", which translates as "basic healthcare doctor". I hate initialisms because if you haven't learned what they stand for, most of the time they are impossible to understand. Polish has very few of them, and when they do become common, like POZ, they always annoy me. Language should make communication easier, not harder, and brevity should never be more important than making things clear even to those not in the know.

I didn't know AMMAN was called Philadelphia millennia ago but I liked the clue. It made me think. Obviously the Hellenistic name pointed to a city in Alexander the Great's and his successors' domain that is a current capital, which narrowed things down. The first cross or two made it obvious it would be Amman.

I noticed a new feature in the puzzle. The next available box usual just turns yellow- now it has a black border. This border covers the bottom of the letter above, which messes me up when doing Down clues. For example the bottom of an L is covered and it looks like an I.  Anyone else have this issue?

After my first pass through all of the clues I really thought this was going to be a DNF for me. But thanks mainly to the long answers it started sloooowly coming together. The SW corner was the last to fall for me.

I really ended up enjoying the heck out of this one. Very difficult for me, but not impossible. :)

Mr. Rafael Musa, when you say "I'll be back soon," I hope you are making a promise! And so, need I say again how much I adore Rafa's puzzles? I love the dichotomy between the smartly convoluted clues and the amazing simplicity of the entries. It always makes me start out thinking "I'm never going to solve this grid" and end up saying "Hah! That was pretty obvious after all." (But no, it really wasn't until it was.) There's also much that's conversational in Rafa's puzzles, so it always inspires me to talk to myself – and sometimes to him – out loud. "How do you expect me to know that?" "Oh, wow, NANTES, how did I get that from just the middle N?" "Huh? Ptolemeic royal? Are you joking? Oh, okay, CLEO, my good friend..." In other words, I have tons of fun with Musa grids, and this one was no different. Thank you, Rafa! P.S. I couldn't see LET BE in the puzzle and not think of these four blokes (who I doubt were ever just a GARAGE BAND in Liverpool...) – https://youtu.be/CGj85pVzRJs?is=vBUvWNXbDQGrzELM

I found this pretty simple but not obviously burdened by the fickle finger of easening.  (Though it seems even Musa is not immune to meddling).  XWStats users say Average at the moment, so yeah.

As is often with longer answers/spanners, those came almost too quickly but were interesting.

I admit that both the upper left and lower right gave me pause and crunch, with the upper left more frightening.  I will say that "enemy spies" feels just a little forced to me.

In all I enjoyed this puzzle and look forward to more.

"Your goats and sheep know macramé?"
"I kid ewe knot!"

(It just struck a cord with them.)
Awesome and fun! Loved all the misdirects. Especially "duds"!! 😂

Rafael, you know how to a-Musa recalcitrant  batch of solvers (at least, for the most part) avec les catchy clues.  CAVA rings a welcome bell that reminds me of happy times in Madrid.

An alternate clue for 57A could have been "A humbling dessert" = ENEMYS' PIES, but the one you used was just fine.

Thank you, and come back soon.  We'll be waiting

As a non USA solver, I loved this puzzle! 

It relied so much on clever wordplay, such fun answers, almost every entry is a pun or a twist of some kind on words in a simple and elegant way. 

Even though its a Friday puzzle and it wasnt at all trivial, its so refreshing to see interesting and odd words instead of obscure baseball trivia or NBA/NFL/MLB player names.

 Loved this, really hope we see more of you Rafa!!
rock solid puzzle pun intended - reference to ACME is so timely as well.  the film about poor Wiley Coyete's failed purchases is in theaters.  thanks Rafael this is why we love to solve crosswords!
Johnny Carson at 14 across! : D
Great cluing for the company known for duds and the sources of rock
Perfect Friday. Very little on the first pass. Got a handful of gimmes and it fell like a house of cards.
Chewy. Good stuff!
Nice puzzle Rafa.  And "celli" is definitely a legit plural word so don't stress about it!

A very solvable, Robyn-esque Friday puzzle, Rafa. I enjoyed it very much, but did myself in in the NW corner. I couldn't get past Dinner DATE to get to TINDER DATE and was afraid to commit to CANOE even though I had a hunch. Oh, well. One thing I was positive about was the U2 producer. Too bad he didn't produce this one featuring the late, great BB King. Jimmy Iovine did. https://youtu.be/_TGU35i8czo?si=L7gfgoz-s5lyi7UB Better jump that train.
I kid you not, the NW corner was tough!
Having PCP as the solution for "go to doc" made no sense to this non-American. We have GPs. We also have PCP which may well send you to a GP, or a hospital emergency room.

Nice challenge for a Friday. Bit of toil required to begin with, then a nice downhill run from then on. Well done to the constructor!

I ended up having to start at the bottom right, which was ironically where I got stuck for the longest time after competing the rest. 

We call our 'PCP' a General Practitioner (GP) here... Had to go through the alphabet to get psst. My mind refused to reconsile the answer to the clue. The capitalised 'P' had me fooled! 😬
Cluing was weak (I took longer than my average) -- 2 out of 5 Grant R stars
A Good Friday challenge… eyelets was clever.
Nice puzzle, but to me stew goes *in* a ladle.
Easy week or am I getting better? Decent cluing but I would've expected something slightly more complicated for a Friday. Still a lot of fun: thanks!

60 across showed a Catholic bias. The Devil is one of many Tarot cards, so the Tarot is NOT the Devil's "domain." I thought the Catholic Church got over that nonsense that card reading was evil. Asking Pope Leo: Are we over that yet. (P.S. Dissenting Catholic here.)
A lovely puzzle with a lot of silly nonsense in the south-east.

The Wordplay column says: "I’ll be the first to admit I’ve never seen or heard the word CELLI, but everywhere I consulted assured me it was an accepted plural." From my limited study of Italian, i can tell you that plurals in Italian are "molto regolare"--very regular, like clockwork. A singular word that ends in "o" forms the plural with "i." And a singular word that ends in "a" forms the plural with "e." There you go: one ragazzo, two ragazzi. one ragazza, two ragazze. Boys and girls together: ragazzi. "East side, west side, all around the town The tots play ring-around-Rosie, London Bridge is falling down. Boys and girls together, me and Mamie O'Rourke Tripped the light fantastic on the sidewalks of New York" Very famous song.... https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bbhkS4VGGpI
The lower right was nigh impossible.

That felt hard until the clues started to fill in from the midpoint down. Love the long spans.
I had no idea what PCP was until I read a few posts. Ok, so like the Aussies we have GP’s (General Practitioners). Good luck trying to see one these days though, rarer than hens teeth in these parts.

Nice Friday puzzle with some clever misdirects.  I hope Rafael was serious about being back soon.

Since I just saw Coyote vs ACME a couple of weeks ago, that one went in without a second thought.

In other news,
I YOTE YES on eliminating question marks on Friday and Saturday unless it's an actual question.
Wow I can finally be proud and say I also thought the Friday was easy but I was stuck on SONK for a while because I didn’t know CELLO was not plural

I enjoyed the flow of this puzzle. Needed a few searches to complete. Because I had zip for pep and ant hill instead of nest I found Zara tights fit nicely for 'ones providing brief assistance' before I figured out paralegals. And I had DISH awhile at 58 across, as I don't think too many kosher families actually have two sinks.
I don't like the new yellow square. It blocks parts of the other letters, making it hard to see the entire word. Please get rid of it.
I'm assuming it's pure coincidence that at least two crosses of TINDERDATE have nothing to with what can happen on one.
Very satisfying puzzle. Initial passes yielded very little, then a couple key words triggered an avalanche of answers with no pesky last squares.

The Door – that answer you get that breaks things open, where your brow is knit in struggle to find an opening anywhere, then you suddenly flash on an answer that was eluding you, and from there, new answers spread, sometimes pop-pop-pop, and soon after, you’re looking at a completed grid, and you’re thinking, “What just happened?”

From still to thrill.

As usual for Rafael, this puzzle was top flight:

I KID YOU NOT, GAME THE SYSTEM, THAT REMINDS ME, BE RIGHT BACK, BANAL, AVERSE, CATCHY, GAPE, CUDDLE.

[National company known for its duds], for ACME.
[Focus for the foul-mouthed?] for ORAL HEALTH.

Hardly a hint of junk despite the full house of excellent answers.  An uber-flowy grid design.  Humor and variety.  I saw that bell on the desk.  I was fooled into thinking “skiing” for [Olympic slalom equipment].  I pictured Wile E. Coyote pressing down the TNT plunge detonator.

Some constructors are simply top flight every. Single. Time.  Thank you for a splendid outing, Rafael.
Weird. I went from stumped to solved in pretty short order; I've never had such a bad first pass fall into place so quickly. A sign of skillful authorship, I would say.

Beaut of a puzz.

Loved it.

Always love seeing RM 
right before I crack it open
and dive in.

Apparently, 
I’m diving into…

an egg..?

Happy Friday all.
Nice Friday! NW corner stumped me for a while, but time away from the puzzle did the trick. MARY JANE is a refreshing new one. Good construction 👍

Not throwing any shade on Mr. Musa’s work — it was quite the satisfying journey from “What the…?” to “Ohhh!” — but my prize for the day goes to Mr. McGowan’s “Wordplay” commentary on 49D.  I’ll be smiling about that all day!

Also lovely to see the plural of my first non-keyboard instrument included.  Yes, fans, CELLI is plural just as PANINI is.  Um, are.  Well, you get the drift.

Have a lovely day, fellow cruciverbalists, and remember to be kind.
I stuck with DINNERDATE waaay too long. Great workout Rafael – thanks!
Thought I was real cute sticking IKNOWRIGHT in with no crosses for 14A. Unsuprisingly, NW took me a while. Fun solve!

If you want to display your digital maps using a different projection, there is always the Amercator Projection. It preserves area, but occasionally distorts names…


A very enjoyable Friday puzzle! Only exploded when it was supposed to!
Good Friday puzzle, I needed help to complete it but that’s on me! Respect for EYELETS and slalom = CANOE

I seem to be an outlier here. Started at 1A and thought, oh no, this is going to be one tough Friday. But then I whooshed through the entire puzzle. Ended up back at 1A and filled in the missing N. I was pretty sure it was correct, since the last name of 3D was Italian. I solve on paper, so no indication until I got here. The crosses helped a lot, and those long answers just jumped out at me. 

Having said that, the clues were delightful and the puzzle on the whole was very clever, even though I thought it was Wednesday-ish.

A solidly Good puzzle.  Put up more than a little resistance.

Not as impressed with the clueing as some of you.  Some seemed to me to be trying too hard, but that's very subjective.  When some land with a thud it tends to detract from those that connected.  Reminds me of "What to leave in, what to leave out?"
Interestingly, the butler doing it isn’t actually very common. It’s what’s known as a dead unicorn trope: a cliche that was never really used much.

A proper crossword, hooray!
Apart from the supermodel - I don't know any models, super or not, some great clues, like BANAL, the plants, loopholes. the bands. 
Very nice.
dINnERDATE got me confused for far too long.
Fun puzzle. ENO, NINO, TINDER killed the goldstar. Oh well. Friday is the new Saturday so it's mimosa time. Cheers!

PLEASE GET RID OF THE BLACK BOX SURROUNDING THE HIGHLIGHTED SQUARE!! Yes, yelling in frustration. It partly obscures the adjacent letters! It totally detracts from the flow of doing the puzzle. It is senseless; the highlight is *plenty*.  I've sent multiple comments. The box is still there. Please please make it go away!
Fun puzzle. That southeast corner was a challenge, though! I got stuck with ANTHILL and ANTFARM before finally figuring out what to call their home. PSST, the rest fell rather quickly, then.

ANTHILL and BEEHIVE both fit in there perfectly well...
ASK POLITELrats
Invasive plants?  Hoo, boy!  How long have you got?
I carried a "start" from my Ohio neighbor's Obedient Plant (a mannerly 12-18") to my Arkansas flowerbeds...where it became a six-foot juggernaut, ruthlessly spreading vigorously.  The ultimate remedy was moving away....

The tricky clues were fun.  Great Saturday puzzle... 
 although "Ganja" sounds like an adjective meaning "Really big."  Tsk

Nice Friday puzzle. Good workout, but... just got stuck in a couple of places and couldn't quite work it all out. Apparently that's just me. No big deal. Anyway... puzzle find today. A Sunday from April 18, 2010 by Randolph Ross with the title: "Whats-its." Some theme clue and answer examples (and the clues all had an asterisk at the beginning): "Uncle" - SAYIT "Your tongue" - BITEIT "An idea" - COMETOTHINKOFIT "The picture" - GETIT "Crow" - EATIT "The light" - SEEIT "Face" - LOSEIT "The point" - STICKTOIT "A deck of cards" - DEALWITHIT "The aisles" - ROLLINGINIT "Lunch" - BROWNBAGIT "An abacus" - COUNTONIT "Snuff" - NOTUPTOIT And there were more. Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=4/18/2010&h=23a ...

I loved, LOVED the My Brilliant Friend books, and funnily enough that was the last clue to drop for me, *and* only after brute forcing it.  For the life of me I couldn't remember the character's name!  I find that to be the case even with some of my all-time favorite books though, save for Lizzie Bennett and her ilk.
Does anyone else hate the new square border? I find it very distracting.

Here's an analogy.  "This puzzle is to words as CATCHY is to melody."  Enjoyable enough, chatty and playful enough, that I was sorry when it was over.

The first thing it did was incite curiosity -- one of my favorite occurrences.  As a one-time Editor of The Mystery Guild, I had no idea what word the whodunit where the butler did it would be.  Looked at it one way, it could be predictable, a snooze, a cliche.  OTOH, it could be ironic, jokey, even a double twist.  (The movie "Murder By Death" makes it an inside joke; Agatha would have made it a double twist ending.) 
 
I would have seen BANAL earlier, but I was stymied by initially having BASE instead of GEAR at 10A.

Two questions:  Don't slalom races take place on snow, whereas CANOE events take place on water?  I don't really get 1A.  And I sort of don't get the ORAL HEALTH wordplay (15D).  The ORAL, yes, but the HEALTH, no.

Doesn't matter.  The fill is colorful and the cluing is playful and imaginative and I had a very good time.

I bet Philadelphia Phillies baseball cards from nearly two millennia ago are extremely rare and valuable.

Back when the World Series really was worldwide.

I thought this puzzle would be difficult, and it was, but enjoyably so. I have only read one mystery novel where the butler did it, an old Mary Roberts Rinehart. I went through a phase reading all of her books. I remember they were fun, and they may have been clichéd. Not really banal though.

Wonderful puzzle! Amazingly, while solving it and have those, "Hmm, no idea here... oh wait, I know!" moments that make crosswords fun, I wondered at how Weintraubian it was. But we had one from her not that long ago, so I was curious as to the constructor. What a thing to read those notes and see a connection I hadn't guessed.

I hardly ever finish a Friday but I got this one in 27m, which is good for me! I feel like I’m finally getting a grip on the longer answers like ENEMYSPIES and THATREMINDSME. They’re certainly tougher than the shorter ones, but that makes it all the more satisfying to get them. Had lots of fun with this!

Once more as a PSA:
We all hate the new current-square highlight box. Mine's orange, yours is black, somebody else's is a wavering blue line (?), apparently?

Try tapping or clicking in the white space surrounding the grid. 
I have to do it each time, but the offending bugfeature disappears.

Good luck!
If it works for you, you're welcome!
Thank you, Rafa, for a fun, fine Friday grid!! I hope we won't need to wait too long for your next one!😊

How do you know if you are anywhere near for enough for the crossword puzzle competition? I've improved a lot over the years, and I know the very top solvers would blow me out of the water, but where's the line for the rest of the competition?? For example, what's a good competitor time for this puzzle??
Awesome themeless Wednesday puzzle
"What?," he said, "You mean Greenland isn't really that big?"

This time it's LADLE. Each time I do the different levels of crossword puzzles on the same day, there's at least one random word that appears in at least 2 puzzles. 

It may be chance, but it's weird

Having done NYT crossword puzzles for most of my long adult life, I am still amazed by two things. One, they just keep coming, each a challenging and unique creation, with or without a theme. How lucky we are to have this infinite scroll to enjoy each day! Two, when unable to get the last few letters or a large section of the puzzle, when really stuck, if I leave it for a few hours or overnight, 99% of the time I can complete it quickly when I return. It's amazing what a fresh mind and outlook can do!

Found this appropriately challenging for a Friday; solved it without help but took about 35 minutes.

Didn't find the fill or cluing all that interesting, but felt like I'd accomplished something when I finished.

Getting all the cities rather easily helped me today.
Can someone please explain to me the clue, "Doesn't feel so hot," in the Midi?  Answer is "AILS." 17 Down.  This is driving me crazy.

Very fine Friday challenge, especially that NW quadrant. There's slalom CANOE now? I thought it was called whitewater. I can usually judge a puzzle's difficulty by whether I can get 1A right off the jump, and that one was a doozy. Then the Spanish sparkling wine. Ay caramba! But here's my CATCHY earworm, courtesy of The Clash: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UpapNzYkxNE

Nice, loved it. Not knowing cava was my last letter, I had “huddle” instead of “cuddle”—that works, right? lol. 
The long answers were so clever. 🙂

Fun puzzle with some great clues and long answers! I haven’t seen it commented so I’ll mention that I also liked seeing the first Freudian stage (the ORAL of ORALHEALTH) placed close by the second. Serendipitous or deliberate?

Hi Rafa! If you're going to be so twee as to use the Italian plural, you should spell it " 'celli," with the apostrophe--the word is, in fact, an abbreviation for "violoncelli." (In orchestral scores, it's usually abbreviated "Vc" or "V-c.," although snotty French scores will use "Velles.," for "Violoncelles.") Here's a catchy earworm, care of the great* Estonian composer Arvo Pärt: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I7rcDZuZBkg&list=RDI7rcDZuZBkg&start_radio=1 *Actually, Pärt is just average sized--he just appears great because he's from so far north. Great puzzle, Rafa--thank you!

This was a Friday record for me, but I ruined it for myself. I finished yesterdays this morning and opened XWordStats to see the difficulty but the google link sent me to todays. I saw CANOE and CAVA before I realised it was the wrong day. I'd have gotten CANOE I think after a bit of thinking and the fact that the same clue came up recently-ish. No way I'd have got CAVA, even though I think that came up recently too.
A very sprightly Friday...with delightful cluing. Grazie, Rafael!

I always do the easier version of Friday’s puzzle. For some reason I don’t think I got the easier clues. I did what I always do. Went to the email from NYT and pressed on play easier version. Instead of going directly on to the puzzle it sent me to the regular place and I picked Crossword. Was the Easier Mode not working or was it my brain?

It's interesting to see that this is a puzzle that seems to be universally liked by the commenters. There is more unanimity than I think I've seen before. There seem to be a very few people who feel that the puzzle was a little too easy. 

But as much as a unanimous winner as I've ever noticed in my about-a-year doing puzzles. 

I like the cleverness of the answers and the AHA nature of it. As a newbie, I have to admit that I did need some lookups, (especially as I worked on it n the middle of he night).

Scanned the comments, and I seem to be alone in not connecting "GO-TO DOC" with the response. Had to get it via the crosses. Anyone care to clear it up for me? 

Loved the puzzle!

One of my most satisfying solves! 3 Fridays in a row which is probably a first for me.

I’ve been doing these on and off for years, but only really started getting the hang of it lately. I love the feeling of staring at a mostly blank grid and having the confidence that I can figure it out rather than just surrendering too quickly.

I see I'm not the only one who wanted IKnowrighT in the upper left. Took way too long to recover from that.

In the process of letting that go, I tried a little of everything for giving one's approval, including noting it, signing it, even miming it. 

MIMES YES does have a silent ring to it, does it not?

I may need to credit Taylor Swift for today’s poem…

‘cause it loves me

a/ like a cat speaking
to a cat in 
“cat”
that is d/ what’s known as “that”
the way you say
a/ yes yes
you nest… me lap
yes yes
be right back

"Cava" seemed to bedevil some folks, but most happily a number of us have imbibed it. 
It's a fine, economical choice (as are many Spanish wines) if your local liquor store carries it.

Found this one very enjoyable, as is always my experience with Mr. Musa's puzzles! Was a bit tough for me in some areas, many this before thats, but finished up in average time with no actual stress, crunchy, but no need to despair or be tempted to GAMETHESYSTEM. 

Though I first thought of tAbLE for 20A, I liked that LADLE the answer crossed "Spoon" the clue. 

For the "Outcome of a match," I put garage fire and thought I was very clever to not fall for thinking it was a sports match. Ha! Hopefully, the BAND got out of the GARAGE before the match got struck....  Har!  

Enjoyed all the long entries and MR X (misdirects, for those who are not fluent in my voice to text capabilities, or lack thereof). 

Alas, with the changing of the weather, flip flops will not be able to be my footwear of choice after any and every given procedure for much longer, but....  my PEDI appointment is scheduled and we are set to sail in less than two weeks, so I get to extend the season a bit longer while we embark into our 22nd year of marriage. Whoohoooo!!!

Loved this puzzle by Rafael Musa. I first had
I Know righT? for I KID YOU NOT and like somebody else here I had diNnER DATE for
TINDER DATE. Was a fun puzzle 🧩 , thanks!

I guess I am in the minority again but found this one a huge slog. Admittedly some due to just being on a different wavelength than the constructor but also for having, imho, too much esoteric trivia and overly erudite clueing that is only helpful in solving crossword puzzles that was not helped by any crosses, at least for me. I will be happy if I never see a puzzle from this constructor again. At least it got some of the pretentious commenters who claim everything is too easy to quit whining for a day.

A little easy for a Friday, but I didn’t have much time anyway, and I enjoyed it.

I’m not a rabbi, and even if I were, I wouldn’t have “the” answer. If you talk to any two rabbis, you’ll get three opinions on anything. 

As mandated in the Torah, the only thing that is banned  is to boil a kid (i.e, a baby goat) in its mother’s milk, but that has generally been broadened to no meat (including birds, which aren’t even mammals) and dairy of any kind together. How many hoops you go through is up to how rigorous you (and your rabbi) strive to be. 

Obviously, those with less means don’t have two of everything. But they may not cook, wash, store, etc. meat and dairy together. The fridge may have separate shelves for each. The oven may have an upper and lower compartment. The cooktop can be divided, two for meat, two for dairy. Two sinks in separate locations is better, but if it isn’t feasible, a double sink is OK. Just not “wash in one, rinse in the other.”  You have to dedicate one side for meat, one for milk, no crossover, with two different drain boards. 

Kosher households may have red plastic containers for meat leftovers , blue ones for dairy, and clear ones for anything else (pareve, meaning neither meat nor milk, so acceptable with either). 

That being said, many less observant Jews around the world are fine with a cheeseburger and a milkshake. Not a baby goat to be found. As I said, three opinions.
